newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook - Diesel sellers look West.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook - Diesel sellers look West.

text.p: Rock bottom Asian gas oil prices might have encouraged scattered cargo movements westward, reversing a trend seen only three months ago when prices here were the best in the world, traders said on Monday.
They said a major oil company might have sold at least one cargo to a trader bound for South America at a premium level to Singapore spot quotes, free-on-board (fob) Singapore basis.
The major might also be working on moving cargoes to South America or Africa, traders said.
Bur traders said the volumes of gas oil being shipped westward are to small to conclude that the arbitrage window from Asia has opened.

But they noted that if current meagre demand and depressed prices in Asia persisted, it would encourage more suppliers to look for markets outside Asia in a frantic attempt to soak up excess supplies and boost flagging prices.
They said that prompt gas oil values might have almost reached its bottom at the current $19.80-$20.00 range, with the support placed at $19.50, which is a three-year low.

Despite cuts in crude runs at two Singapore refiners, while other refiners not pushing operating rates at fuill throttle, middle-distillate stocks here rose by 720,000 barrels to 11.464 million barrels for the week ended July 9.
Traders attributed this to refiners' difficulties to get buyers to mop up their supplies.
They said that scattered buying by China has not excited the market as the mainland remained reluctant to commit themselves to import large volumes during the second half of the year.
Chinese buyers last week bought small gas oil parcels at around $155-$156 per tonne, cost-and-freight southern China and at $153-$154 later in the week.
But this was offset by talk that Chinese refiners aimed to sell to Hong Kong at around $150 per tonne.

Some demand is seen from Indonesia and Nepal for August. Indonesia was said to have started buying for its August requirements, estimated at around five million, while Nepal seeks two 0.5-percent sulphur gas oil cargoes for that month in a tender which closes on Tuesday.
Sri Lanka would also issue a tender this week to buy gas oil and jet fuel for early August delivery.
Jet fuel would continue to track gas oil in its downtrend with traders seeing near term prompt support at $21.50 per barrel, fob basis.

As expected, India failed to bring cheer to the market, limiting its August spot import to one cargo. The 45,000-tonne cargo was purchased from a US major at a three-cent premium, on a c-and-f basis to the Indian east coast.
But traders remained optimistic that state-owned Indian Oil Corp (IOC) might reissue its term tender to buy kerosene and gas oil for an eight-month period.

Naphtha prices extended its gains last week and maintained its backwardation despite market scepticism of its bull run, while gasoline was steady, unaffected by news of South Korean sales to Saudi Arabia.
But firmer naphtha levels and stagnant gasoline prices were putting more pressure on reforming margins, with the spread between the two light distillates much lower than $2.00 per barrel.
Refiners have already cut reforming output as the spread have fallen below the $4-$5 breakeven costs.

Traders said South Korean Ssangyong's deal to sell 1.8 million barrels of 95-octane gasoline from July-January to Saudi Aramco should ease the pressure on the market but this was not deemed sufficient to boost the oversupplied Asian market.
"At least some cargoes will move out of Asia so there will be less pressure," a gasoline trader said. "But I don't think it will have a major impact with the market so depresssed."

Traders said high sulphur fuel oil prices would remain supported as a Singapore trader, who has already purchased 240,000 tonnes since end June, would continue to buy this week despite being absent on Friday.
They said the 180-centistoke grade would remain rangebound around $99-$100 per tonne.
"He is buying to supply Vietnam, Indonesia and China. The demand is quite stable but not very big," one trader said.
Sentiment remained strong in the low sulphur waxy residue (LSWR) market on tight supplies in July.
Supplies from Indonesia stood at 2.6 million barrels in July, compared with 3.6 million in June, due to refinery maintenance turnaround.
"The $16-per-barrel level should be a solid floor for the market for the rest of this month," one trader said.
